passages.source_text: ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις Εἰ μορφὴν ἔχει, καὶ σχῆμα ἔχει καὶ ἐν τόπῳ ἐστίν· ἐν τόπῳ δὲ ὢν καὶ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ περιεχόμενος ὡς ἥττων, πῶς ὑπὲρ πάντας ἐστὶν μέγας; πῶς δὲ καὶ πανταχῇ εἶναι δύναται, ἐν σχήματι ὤν; πρὸς τὸν ταῦτα λέγοντα πρῶτον ἔστιν εἰπεῖν Τοιαῦτα περὶ αὐτοῦ φρονεῖν πείθουσιν πιστεύειν οἱ περὶ Σίμωνα, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, οὐ κατὰ κέλευσιν τὰς ἀποδείξεις ὑμῖν τοῦ οὕτως ἔχειν ἀνάγκη παρέχειν. πρῶτον δὲ περὶ τόπου ἐρῶ καὶ θεοῦ. τόπος ἐστὶν τὸ μὴ ὄν, θεὸς δὲ τὸ ὄν· τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τῷ ὄντι οὐ συγκρίνεται. πῶς γὰρ τόπος ὢν εἶναι δύναται; ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ δευτέρα χώρα εἴη, οἷον οὐρανός, γῆ, ὕδωρ, ἀὴρ καὶ εἰ ἄλλο τι ἐστὶν σῶμα, ὃ ἂν καὶ αὐτοῦ πληροῦν τὸ κενόν, ὃ διὰ τοῦτο κενὸν λέγεται, ὅτι οὐδέν ἐστιν. τοῦτο γὰρ αὐτῷ (τὸ οὐδέν) οἰκειότερον ὄνομα· τὸ γὰρ λεγόμενον κενὸν τί ποτε ὡς σκεῦός ἐστιν οὐδὲν ἔχον; πλὴν αὐτὸ τὸ σκεῦος κενὸν ὂν οὐκ αὐτό ἐστι τόπος, ἀλλ’ ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν αὐτὸ τὸ κενόν, εἴπερ σκεῦός ἐστιν. ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα τὸ ὂν ἐν τῷ μηδὲν ὄντι εἶναι. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ μὴ ὂν λέγω (ὃ ὑπὸ τινῶν τόπος λέγεται) οὐδὲν ὄν. οὐδὲν δὲ ὂν τῷ ὄντι πῶς συγκρίνεται; ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ ἐν τοῖς ἐναντίοις, ἵνα τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἔστιν τι, πολλῶν παραδειγμάτων σπευδόντων ἐξ ἐμοῦ προελθεῖν εἰς ἀπόδειξιν ἑνὶ μόνῳ χρήσασθαι θέλω, ἵνα δείξω ὅτι οὐ πάντως τὸ περιέχον τοῦ περιεχομένου κρεῖττόν ἐστιν. ὁ ἥλιος σχῆμά ἐστιν περιφερὲς καὶ ὑπὸ ἀέρος ὅλος περιέχεται, ἀλλὰ τοῦτον ἐκλαμπρύνει, τοῦτον θερμαίνει, τοῦτον τέμνει, κἂν ἀπῇ αὐτοῦ, σκότῳ περιβάλλεται, καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται, ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀνατολῆς πάλιν φωτίζεται, καὶ ὅπου ἂν αὐτῷ παραθάλπηται, καὶ κάλλει τῷ μείζονι κοσμεῖται. καὶ ταῦτα ποιεῖ τῇ αὐτοῦ μετουσίᾳ, τὴν οὐσίαν περιωρισμένην ἔχων. τί οὖν ἔτι κωλύει τὸν θεὸν ὡς τούτου καὶ πάντων δημιουργὸν καὶ δεσπότην ὄντα, αὐτὸν μὲν ἐν σχήματι καὶ μορφῇ καὶ κάλλει ὄντα, τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν;

τοῦτό ἐστιν ἑβδομάδος μυστήριον. αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν ὅλων ἀνάπαυσις, ὡς τοῖς ἐν μικρῷ μιμουμένοις αὐτοῦ τὸ μέγα αὐτὸν χαρίζεται εἰς ἀνάπαυσιν. αὐτός ἐστιν μόνος πῇ μὲν καταληπτός, πῇ δὲ ἀκατάληπτος, πῇ μὲν περαντός, πῇ δὲ ἀπέραντος, τὰς ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐκτάσεις ἔχων εἰς ἄπειρον. οὗτος γὰρ καταληπτός ἐστιν καὶ ἀκατάληπτος, ἐγγὺς καὶ μακράν, ὧδε ὢν κἀκεῖ, ὡς μόνος ὑπάρχων καὶ τοῦ πανταχόθεν ἀπείρου νοὸς τὴν μετουσίαν ἔχων, ἣν πάντων ἀναπνέουσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ τὸ ζῆν ἔχουσιν· κἂν χωρισθῶσιν τοῦ σώματος, καὶ τὸν εἰς αὐτὸν εὑρεθῶσιν πόθον ἔχουσαι, εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται, ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου ἀκτίνων ἑλκόμενοι φέρονται πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀθάνατοι. οἷαν οὖν στοργὴν συλλαβεῖν δυνάμεθα, ἐὰν τὴν εὐμορφίαν αὐτοῦ τῷ νῷ κατοπτεύσωμεν; ἄλλως δὲ ἀμήχανον· ἀδύνατον γὰρ κάλλος ἄνευ μορφῆς εἶναι, καὶ πρὸς τὸν αὐτοῦ ἔρωτα ἐπισπᾶσθαί τινα ἢ καὶ δοκεῖν θεὸν ὁρᾶν εἶδος οὐκ ἔχοντα.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Εἰς ἄλλο προτείνας εἰπεῖν, εἰς ἕτερον ἀπεκρίνω· προέτεινας γὰρ ὡς μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ... ἐπιβαλὼν δὲ ἔπειθες ἡμᾶς ὅτι ἀσφαλέστερός ἐστιν ὁ ὑπὸ ὀπτασίας ἀκούων τοῦ παρ’ αὐτῆς ἐναργείας ἀκούοντος. πέρας γοῦν διὰ τοῦτο ἐμοῦ ἱκανώτερον ἔφασκες εἰδέναι τὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὡς ὑπὸ ὀπτασίας αὐτοῦ ἀκηκοὼς τὸν λόγον. πλὴν ἐγὼ εἰς τὸ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς προταθὲν ἀποκρίνομαι. ὁ προφήτης, ὅτι προφήτης ἐστὶν πληροφορήσας πρῶτον, περὶ τῶν ἐναργῶς ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων ἀσφαλῶς πιστεύεται, καὶ ἀληθὴς ὢν προεπιγνωσθεὶς καὶ ὡς ὁ μανθάνων θέλει ἐξετασθεὶς καὶ ἀνακριθεὶς ἀποκρίνεται — ὁ δὲ ὀπτασίᾳ πιστεύων ἢ ὁράματι καὶ ἐνυπνίῳ ἐπισφαλής ἐστιν· ἀγνοεῖ γὰρ τίνι πιστεύει· ἐνδέχεται γὰρ αὐτὸν ἢ δαίμονα κακὸν εἶναι ἢ πνεῦμα πλάνον ἐν τῷ λέγειν ὑποκρινόμενον εἶναι ὃ μὴ ἔστιν. εἰ δ’ ἄρα τις βουληθείη πυνθάνεσθαι τὸ τίς ἂν ὁ φανείς, δύναται λέγειν ἑαυτῷ ὃ βούλεται. καὶ οὕτως ὡς πονηρὸς ἀστράψας, μείνας ὅσον θέλει, ἀποσβέννυται, μὴ παραμείνας τῷ πυνθανομένῳ εἰς ἀνάκρισιν ὅσον ἠθέλησεν. διὰ δὲ ἐνυπνίων ὁρῶν τις οὐδὲ πυνθάνεσθαι δύναται περὶ ὧν βούλεται· οὐ γὰρ ἰδίας ἐξουσίας ἐστὶν ὁ λογισμὸς τοῦ κοιμωμένου. ἔνθεν γοῦν πολλὰ ἡμεῖς ὕπαρ ἐπιθυμοῦντες μαθεῖν κατ’ ὄναρ περὶ ἑτέρων πυνθανόμεθα, ἢ καὶ μὴ πυνθανόμενοι περὶ τῶν μὴ διαφερόντων ἡμῖν ἀκούομεν, καὶ διυπνισθέντες ἀθυμοῦμεν ὅτι περὶ ὧν ἐπεθυμοῦμεν μαθεῖν οὔτε ἠκούσαμεν οὔτε ἐξητάσαμεν.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Εἰ φῂς τὰς ὀπτασίας μὴ πάντως ἀληθεύειν, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε τὰ ὁράματα καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια θεόπεμπτα ὄντα οὐ ψεύδεται, περὶ ὧν ἂν εἰπεῖν θέλῃ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ὀρθῶς ἔφης ὅτι θεόπεμπτα ὄντα οὐ ψεύδεται. ἄδηλον δὲ εἰ ὁ ἰδὼν θεόπεμπτον ἑώρακεν ὄνειρον. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἐὰν ᾖ ὁ ἑωρακὼς δίκαιος, ἀληθὲς ἑώρακεν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ὀρθῶς ἔφης. τίς δὲ δίκαιος, εἰ ὁράματος χρῄζει, ἵνα μάθῃ ἃ δεῖ μαθεῖν καὶ ποιῇ ἃ δεῖ ποιεῖν; καὶ ὁ Σίμων Τοῦτό μοι δὸς ὅτι μόνος ὁ δίκαιος ὅραμα ἀληθὲς ἰδεῖν δύναται, καὶ ἀποκρίνομαί σοι εἰς αὐτό. ἐμοὶ γὰρ κέκριται ὅτι ἀσεβὴς ἀληθῆ ὄνειρον οὐχ ὁρᾷ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Τοῦτο ψεῦδός ἐστιν, καὶ περὶ τούτου ἀγράφως καὶ ἐγγράφως ἀποδεῖξαι δύναμαι, πεῖσαι δὲ οὐκ ἐπαγγέλλομαι. ὁ γὰρ πρὸς ἔρωτα μοχθηρᾶς νεύσας γυναικὸς εἰς ἑτέρας κατὰ πάντα καλῆς συμβίωσιν νόμιμον τὸν ἑαυτοῦ οὐ μετατίθησι νοῦν· ἐνίοτε καὶ ἑαυτοῖς συνειδότες τὴν κρείττονα, προειλημμένοι ἀγαπῶσιν τὴν χείρονα. τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ σὺ πάσχων ἀγνοεῖς. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Παρελόμενος ταῦτα, εἰς ἃ ἐπηγγείλω λέγε. ἐμοὶ γὰρ ἀδύνατον εἶναι δοκεῖ ἀσεβεῖς ἀνθρώπους ὑπὸ θεοῦ ᾡδήποτε ὀνειροπολεῖσθαι τρόπῳ.

πλὴν ὅτι καὶ ἀσεβεῖς ὁράματα καὶ ἐνύπνια ἀληθῆ βλέπουσιν, δῆλόν ἐστιν καὶ ἐγγράφως ἀποδεῖξαι δύναμαι. πέρας γοῦν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται, ὡς ὁ Ἀβιμέλεχ (ἀσεβὴς ὤν, τὴν τοῦ δικαίου Ἀβραὰμ γυναῖκα ἐπὶ κοινωνίᾳ μιᾶναι θελήσας) ἤκουσεν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ καθ’ ὕπνον (ὡς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει) μὴ θιγεῖν αὐτῆς, ὅτι ἀνδρὶ συνῳκηκυῖά ἐστιν. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ Φαραὼ (ἀσεβὴς ἀνήρ) ἑώρακεν ὄνειρον περί τε πυρῶν εὐφορίας καὶ ἀφορίας, ᾧ ὁ Ἰωσὴφ ἐπιλύων παρὰ θεοῦ ἔφη τὸν ὄνειρον γεγενῆσθαι. Ναβουχοδονόσορ δὲ (ὁ εἴδωλα σέβων καὶ τοὺς θεὸν σέβοντας εἰς πῦρ κελεύσας βληθῆναι) ὄνειρον ὅλου μήκους αἰῶνος ὁρᾷ. καὶ μὴ λεγέτω τις Ἀλλ’ ὅραμα ἐγρηγορὼς οὐδεὶς ἀσεβῶν θεωρεῖ. ψεῦδός ἐστιν. αὐτὸς γοῦν ὁ Ναβουχοδονόσορ τρεῖς ἄνδρας κελεύσας βληθῆναι εἰς πῦρ, ἐνιδὼν τῇ καμίνῳ τέταρτον ἔφη „τὸν τέταρτον ὁρῶ ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ“. καὶ ὅμως ὀπτασίας τε καὶ ὁράματα καὶ ἐνύπνια ὁρῶντες ἀληθῆ ἀσεβεῖς ἦσαν. οὗτος οὐ πάντως ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾶν τινὰ ὁράματα καὶ ἐνύπνια καὶ ὀπτασίας πάντως εὐσεβής ἐστιν. τῷ γὰρ εὐσεβεῖ ἐμφύτῳ καὶ καθαρῷ ἀναβλύζει τῷ νῷ τὸ ἀληθές, οὐκ ὀνείρῳ σπουδαζόμενον, ἀλλὰ συνέσει ἀγαθοῖς διδόμενον.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.

passages.text: But someone will say, “If he has a form, he also has a shape and is in a place. If he is in a place and contained by it as something lesser, how is he great above all? And how can he be everywhere while having a shape?” To the person saying this, one can first say: those around Simon persuade people to believe such thoughts about him; but we know to be true the things attested by our Lord Jesus Christ. We are not obliged to provide you at a command with proofs that things are so. But first I will speak about place and God. Place is what does not exist, whereas God is what exists; and what does not exist cannot be compared with what exists. For how can place have existence, unless it is a second region, such as heaven, earth, water, air, or any other body, which would also fill the void there? It is called void for this reason: because it is nothing. Nothing is a more suitable name for it. For what is the so-called void—some sort of vessel that contains nothing? Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, if it is a vessel, place is that in which the empty vessel itself is. For what exists must necessarily be in what is nothing. This is what I mean by what does not exist, which some call place: it is nothing. How can what is nothing be compared with what exists, except as opposites, so that what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is? But even if it is something, although many examples press to come forth from me as proof, I wish to use just one, to show that what contains is not invariably stronger than what is contained. The sun is a circular shape and is wholly contained by air, but it illuminates the air, heats it, and cuts through it. When the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness, and wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying. But at the sun’s rising it is illuminated again, and wherever it is warmed by the sun it is also adorned with greater beauty. The sun does these things by its presence, although its substance is bounded. What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and everything, from himself having shape, form, and beauty, while the presence proceeding from him extends infinitely?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: we know to be true the things attested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine plural has no expressed noun; things or statements attested expresses the ellipsis without adding an extra source claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is
lexical_decisions.rationale: Understands place from the second clause as the predicate to the first, not an assertion that what exists ceases to exist.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording says bright, not dark. The resulting physical description is puzzling, but the main text preserves that printed adjective rather than silently emending it to fit the argument. Its referent is understood as a part of the air.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the presence proceeding from him extends infinitely
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετουσία can be presence, participation, or communicated influence. Presence preserves the analogy with the bounded sun’s effects without adding a second bodily substance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ ἂν καὶ αὐτοῦ πληροῦν τὸ κενόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which would also fill the void there
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῦ locatively, there, referring to the discussed place or region. It is not nominative emphatic αὐτό, itself. A genitive alternative is which would also fill its void, with the precise possessive referent drawn from the surrounding body/region discussion; no replacement Greek is adopted.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
source_issues.issue: The wording associates becoming bright with cooling, which is puzzling in this analogy. Bright is nevertheless what the supplied text says; no emendation to dark has been made.

passages.text: This is the mystery of the sevenfold order. For he himself is the rest of all things, so that to those who imitate his greatness on a small scale he grants himself as rest. He alone is in one respect graspable and in another ungraspable, in one respect bounded and in another unbounded, having the extensions from him reaching into infinity. For he is graspable and ungraspable, near and far, being here and there, existing alone and possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side. By breathing this, the souls of all have life. Even if they are separated from the body, if they are found to possess longing for him, they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun. What affection, then, can we conceive if we behold the beauty of his form with our mind? Otherwise it is impossible: for beauty cannot exist without form, nor can anyone be drawn toward love of him or even imagine seeing God if he has no form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑβδομάδος μυστήριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: mystery of the sevenfold order
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑβδομάς is a group of seven or a week. Sevenfold order retains the six extensions plus rest discussed just before; mystery of the week is a viable more familiar alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ πανταχόθεν ἀπείρου νοὸς τὴν μετουσίαν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετουσία can be participation, presence, or shared influence. Communicating presence retains its life-imparting reach in the breathing clause, without silently identifying a second deity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: they are carried ... into his embrace
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόλπος is bosom or lap; embrace makes the intimate image readable while retaining a personal destination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: just as in winter the vapors of the mountains
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the vapor simile and its mountain origin, without a modern scientific correction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται, ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου ἀκτίνων ἑλκόμενοι φέρονται πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀθάνατοι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches immortal to the souls because the paragraph concerns their continued life after separation from the body. ἀθάνατοι can grammatically agree with feminine souls or masculine vapors, and its printed position after the simile permits the local alternative the vapors ... are carried toward the sun, immortal. Moving the adjective to the souls is a disclosed attachment choice, not uniquely established by morphology.

passages.text: Peter said, “You proposed to speak to one point but answered another. For you proposed that someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ... But then you went on to persuade us that the person hearing from an apparition is more secure than the one hearing from direct perception itself. Indeed, this was why you asserted that you knew Jesus’ teachings more adequately than I, as someone who had heard the word from him through an apparition. Nevertheless I answer the point proposed at the beginning. Once the prophet has first given assurance that he is a prophet, he is securely believed concerning what he says directly; having first been recognized as truthful, he answers after being examined and questioned as the learner wishes. But someone who trusts an apparition, a vision, or a dream is in danger, for he does not know whom he trusts. It is possible that this is an evil demon or a deceptive spirit, pretending in its speech to be what it is not. If someone should wish to inquire who the one appearing is, the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself. Thus, flashing like an evil being and remaining as long as it wishes, it is extinguished, without staying for the questioner’s examination as long as the questioner wanted. Someone who sees through dreams cannot even inquire about what he wishes, for the sleeper’s reasoning is not under his own control. This is why, though we desire to learn many things while awake, in a dream we ask about other things, or, without even asking, hear about things of no concern to us. On waking we are discouraged that we neither heard about nor examined what we desired to learn.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: Better able separately represents μᾶλλον with δύνασθαι, while understand more represents πλεῖον with νοεῖν. Exactly six and three printed gap dots remain; no missing words are restored. The comparison is retained, with indeed representing γάρ in the interrupted construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δύναται λέγειν ἑαυτῷ ὃ βούλεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of δύναται is unstated. The main text takes the apparition as subject, interpreting the dative as speaking on its own behalf, with self-description inferred from the preceding identity question. About itself is not claimed as the literal meaning of ἑαυτῷ. A materially different reading takes the questioner as subject and the reflexive as to himself: If someone wishes to inquire who the appearing figure is, he can tell himself whatever he wishes. The following evanescent apparition favors the main subject continuation, but does not eliminate the alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ δαίμονα κακὸν εἶναι ἢ πνεῦμα πλάνον
lexical_decisions.chosen: an evil demon or a deceptive spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both alternatives remain distinct.

source_issues.source_quote: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
source_issues.issue: Six dots and then three dots mark two printed gaps. Both exact counts remain, without restoring the missing wording or hiding the interrupted syntax.

passages.text: Simon said, “If you say that apparitions do not always speak truth, nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say.” Peter said, “You said correctly that, being sent by God, they do not lie. But it is unclear whether the person who saw it has seen a God-sent dream.” Simon said, “If the person who saw it is righteous, he has seen something true.” Peter said, “You said correctly. But who is righteous if he needs a vision to learn what he ought to learn and to do what he ought to do?” Simon said, “Grant me this, that only the righteous person can see a true vision, and I will answer you on that point. For I have decided that an impious person does not see a true dream.” Peter said, “This is false, and I can demonstrate it both without writing and from writing, though I do not promise to persuade you. For a man who has inclined toward love of a wicked woman does not transfer his mind to lawful life together with another who is good in every way. Sometimes, even knowing in themselves which is better, because they are already captivated they love the worse one. You too are suffering something like this without knowing it.” Simon said, “Leave these things aside and speak to what you promised. For it seems impossible to me for impious people to be given dreams by God in any manner.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγράφως καὶ ἐγγράφως
lexical_decisions.chosen: both without writing and from writing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between proof apart from written texts and proof from them, not between illiteracy and literacy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προειλημμένοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: because they are already captivated
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preoccupation or prior capture explains the persistence in an inferior attachment; no explicit compulsion beyond the source is added.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὖν γε τὰ ὁράματα καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια θεόπεμπτα ὄντα οὐ ψεύδεται, περὶ ὧν ἂν εἰπεῖν θέλῃ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: He understands God as the subject of θέλῃ, chosen because God is the sender encoded in θεόπεμπτα. The subject is not expressly named. About whatever they wish to say is a material alternative with visions and dreams as subject, since a neuter plural can take a singular verb, as the immediately preceding ψεύδεται does. Neither reading requires correcting the supplied text.

passages.text: Nevertheless, that even impious people see true visions and dreams is clear, and I can prove it from writing. For it is written in the law that Abimelech—being impious and having wished to defile the wife of righteous Abraham through intercourse—heard from God in sleep, as the scripture says, not to touch her because she was living with a husband. Pharaoh too, an impious man, saw a dream about abundance and scarcity of wheat; Joseph, explaining it to him, said that the dream had come from God. Nebuchadnezzar, who revered idols and ordered those who revered God to be thrown into fire, saw a dream concerning an age’s whole length. And let no one say, “But no impious person beholds a vision while awake.” That is false. Nebuchadnezzar himself, after ordering three men to be thrown into fire, saw a fourth in the furnace and said, “I see the fourth as a son of God.” Yet although they saw true apparitions, visions, and dreams, they were impious. Such a person is not necessarily reverent simply because he sees visions, dreams, and apparitions. For to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind, not pursued through a dream, but given to good people through understanding.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τέταρτον ὁρῶ ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: I see the fourth as a son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the anarthrous son of God in the quoted statement without identifying the figure as a particular later doctrinal person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὄνειρον ὅλου μήκους αἰῶνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: a dream concerning an age’s whole length
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the broad age-duration wording rather than identifying an unprinted historical timetable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ εὐσεβεῖ ἐμφύτῳ καὶ καθαρῷ ἀναβλύζει τῷ νῷ τὸ ἀληθές
lexical_decisions.chosen: to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjectival grouping can also be taken as in the reverent, inborn, and pure mind; both emphasize inward truth and do not make the dream the source of it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνιδὼν τῇ καμίνῳ τέταρτον ἔφη
lexical_decisions.chosen: saw a fourth in the furnace and said
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέταρτον remains the object of seeing in the narrator’s construction, not merely the subject matter of the subsequent speaking. The following quotation is retained as a separate reported statement.

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological

Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
